Communication-Constrained Parameter Estimation From Overlapping Samples

Goal. Prove the lower envelope by linking estimation error to Fisher information, bounding information from shared and private data, and accounting for the entropy spent on localization.

III. CONVERSE

The lower bound must apply even when processors interact. Its main ingredients are the information in a transcript, a Bayesian risk bound, and the entropy left after the transcript has located the parameter.

A. Score Identities and a Bayesian Inequality

Reading focus. Read the score identity, data processing, trace chain rule, van Trees bound, sample/bit floors, and leftover-entropy budget. Keep the definitions and constants in (85), (86), (96), and (116). The prior integrals (87)-(95) and van Trees proof (97)-(100) can wait once you retain their conclusions in (85) and (101).

1) The score of a processed observation

Guide
What this part does: Derives the score identity: after a θ\thetaθ-free processing, the message score is the conditional mean of the raw score.
Key point: The foundation of the lower bound: compression only averages information away.

To bound what a message can reveal, write its score as the conditional average of the raw-data score.

B IMPORTANTSpeaking · (73) Let'sss start with what a message actually is. We generate raw data first and then randomize or compress it. This integral averages the chance of producing this message over every possible dataset.

1. WhatEven for dependent or nonstandard input, average the message rule against the distribution of the input.2. Where it comes fromCondition on the raw observation Z and integrate the θ-independent kernel K against its density. This is total probability.3. 2) Data processing and the chain rule

Guide
What this part does: Gets the Fisher data-processing inequality from conditional Jensen, then the chain rule.
Key point: Processing adds no information; joint information splits into two parts (III-D uses this for shared data).

Conditional averaging shrinks the score in mean square. When a transcript grows step by step, its score increments contribute through the chain rule.

1. WhatCall the directional signal from raw data SZ​ and the one from the message alone ST​.2. Where it comes fromThese are definitions of the raw-observation score and the processed-observation score.3. Why it mattersNotation for the next linesUsed by(78)What it saysShort names: SZ​ is the raw data's vote, ST​ is the message's vote.

3) A smooth prior on the parameter cube

Guide
What this part does: Picks a smooth prior vanishing at the edges and computes its Fisher information and entropy.
Key point: These two constants feed the van Trees denominator and the entropy budget.

Choose a smooth prior that vanishes on the boundary. This makes the boundary term disappear in the integration-by-parts argument.

B IMPORTANTSpeaking · (85) We now choose a convenient prior on the parameter cube. It vanishes at the boundary and has explicit entropy and information constants. Those two features make the next part of the proof work cleanly.

1. WhatFor the proof, give each coordinate an independent prior that vanishes at both ends. Its entropy and information are explicit.2. Where it comes fromChoose the product sine-squared prior. Its normalization and one-coordinate information/entropy are calculated explicitly in (87)–(95), then added over coordinates.3. Why it mattersIts entropy and Fisher information are explicitUsed by(86), (87), (98), (101), (115), (194)What it saysThe prior used in the proof: each coordinate independently follows 2sin2(πθj​), zero at both ends and high in the middle, like a smooth hill. Its entropy h(π) and Fisher information Jπ​ can both be computed exactly. Careful: π here is both the prior's name and the number 3.14.

4) The Bayesian squared-error inequality

Guide
What this part does: Proves the van Trees inequality by integration by parts and Cauchy–Schwarz.
Key point: Error ≥d2\ge d^2≥d2/(average information + prior information): lower-bounding error = upper-bounding information.

Pair the estimation error with the joint score. Integration by parts gives the signal, and Cauchy–Schwarz turns it into a risk bound.

B IMPORTANTSpeaking · (96) Let'sss switch from prior calculations to estimation error. DDD is the risk averaged over both the random parameter and the observed record.

1. WhatDraw the parameter, then draw its data, and average squared estimation error over both sources of randomness.2. Where it comes fromThis defines the Bayes risk by averaging squared estimation error over the joint prior and observation law.3. Why it mattersThe lower bound is first proved for itUsed by(98), (101)What it saysBayes risk: treat the truth Θ as randomly drawn from the prior too, then average the squared error.

C SKIM PROOFSpeaking · (97) Combine the prior and likelihood into one joint density. Its score is simply the prior score plus the observation score.

1. WhatMultiply the prior density by the data density given the parameter. Taking the log and differentiating produces two terms.2. 5) The accessible-sample lower bound

Guide
What this part does: Computes the expected number of visible samples and gets the first lower bound.
Key point: Even with unlimited communication, error ≳d/min⁡{N,nm}\gtrsim d/\min\{N,nm\}≳d/min{N,nm}.

Even a decoder that sees every accessible observation gets at most one score contribution per distinct observation.

C SKIM PROOFSpeaking · (103) Before communication, ask how much distinct data the network can see. A fixed pool observation is missed only if every machine misses it.

1. WhatOne machine misses a fixed ID with probability 1−m/N. Multiply across machines for the chance they all miss it.2. Where it comes fromEach machine misses a fixed index with probability 1−Nm​. Independence across machines multiplies these n probabilities.3. Why it mattersUsed for the expected number of visible samplesUsed by(104)What it saysThe chance file a is borrowed by nobody: each person skips it with probability 1−m/N, and the n people are independent, so multiply.

6) Parameter information required by small risk

Guide
What this part does: Links error to mutual information: small error forces the transcript to carry much about Θ\ThetaΘ.
Key point: Uses “the Gaussian maximizes entropy for a given variance”.

Small risk forces the posterior to be concentrated. The Gaussian entropy bound turns that concentration into a minimum information requirement.

7) The total-bit floor and conditional entropy budget

Guide
What this part does: BBB bits carry at most BBB bits, giving the bit floor; then split transcript entropy into parameter information and leftover hTh_ThT​.
Key point: The first three lower-bound terms are done; the entropy budget (118) is III-E’s key input.

A transcript of B bits has a limited entropy budget. Once you account for what it must reveal about the parameter, only the remaining conditional entropy is available for the score bound.

C SKIM PROOFSpeaking · (112) The public side information started independently of the parameter. It contributes no information by itself, so only the conditional information in the transcript remains.

1. WhatThe public design and seeds were chosen independently of the parameter. Only the transcript can reveal information once they are given.2. B. Concentration of a Block Score

Reading focus. Understand the event-score bounds (121)-(123), their tail assumptions (120), and the surprisal second moment (139). Read (128) and (130) for the proof idea. Tilt arithmetic (132)-(135) and tail integration (140)-(144) can wait; retain the endpoint bounds, including their conditioning requirements.

1) Conditional means of block scores

Guide
What this part does: Lemma 1: how far learning an event of probability ppp can shift a block score.
Key point: Shift ≲vqln⁡(1/p)+bln⁡(1/p)\lesssim\sqrt{vq\ln(1/p)}+b\ln(1/p)≲vqln(1/p)​+bln(1/p): rarer events say more, but only logarithmically.

Add independent scores into a block score. Conditioning on a rare event can amplify its mean, and the event's surprise measures how much.

What this part does: Bounds the second moment of transcript surprisal uniformly over alphabets with at most 2B2^B2B leaves.

C. Independent Private Blocks

Reading focus. This is the structural heart of the converse. Follow the rectangle (150), product posterior (153), and information sum (159). Important links are (152), (157), (158), (162), and (165): surprisal adds, cross terms cancel, and the bit budget controls the remaining correction. Seed averaging (166)-(167) can wait.

Fix the public and private seeds to make the protocol deterministic. Under independent blocks, each possible transcript imposes one condition on each machine's data.

Product structure of a transcript event

Guide
What this part does: Fixes the complete transcript and all seeds, then factors its event into local checklists.
Key point: With independent inputs at fixed parameter, both leaf probabilities and conditional block laws factor.

A transcript is a checklist: every machine must pass its own checks for that sequence of bits to occur. Independence turns the checklist into a product event.

Each machine now has its own list of required outputs along that path; the intersection checks every turn assigned to it. If it never speaks, its checklist imposes no restriction.

Guide
What this part does: Combines posterior block scores, cancels cross terms after averaging, and applies the single-block event bound.

D. The Additive Shared-Observation Bound

Reading focus. Learn the shared/private partition (170) and the information bounds (174), (176), and (192). Read (172), (181), (182), (184), and (188) to see why the reduction is valid. Averaging steps (185)-(187) can wait. Check the zero-private-data case (191) when that edge case matters.

1) Shared and private observations

Guide
What this part does: Splits samples into a shared group and private groups, and states Theorem 2.
Key point: Shared data add information per item (≤dv\le dv≤dv each); private parts are limited by transcript entropy.

Split the observations by how many processors see them. Shared samples go into one group, and single-owner samples stay in their private blocks.

E. Proof of the Main Lower Bound

Reading focus. Trace (197)+(198) through localization cancellation (202), the scalar log inequality (206), and the refinement floor (219), then combine all floors in (220). Keep the variable changes (200), (205), and the inversion idea (211). Constant calculations (199), (207)-(208), (226), and case algebra (214)-(218) can wait. For the sharper Gaussian branch (221)-(230), focus on (227), the Lambert inverse (229), and the final bound (230).

The three basic risk floors already hold. To get the final term, combine the Fisher bound with the conditional entropy left after localization.
